{{Short description|Group without proper nontrivial characteristic subgroups}}
In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[group theory]], a [[group (mathematics)|group]] is said to be '''characteristically simple''' if it has no proper nontrivial [[characteristic subgroup]]s. Characteristically simple groups are sometimes also termed '''elementary groups'''. Characteristically simple is a ''weaker'' condition than being a [[simple group]], as simple groups must not have any proper nontrivial [[normal subgroup]]s, which include characteristic subgroups.

A [[finite group]] is characteristically simple if and only if it is a [[direct product of groups|direct product]] of [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] simple groups. In particular, a finite [[solvable group]] is characteristically simple if and only if it is an [[elementary abelian group]]. This does not hold in general for [[infinite group]]s; for example, the [[rational number]]s form a characteristically simple group that is not a direct product of simple groups.

A '''minimal normal subgroup''' of a group ''G'' is a nontrivial normal subgroup ''N'' of ''G'' such that the only proper [[subgroup]] of ''N'' that is normal in ''G'' is the trivial subgroup. Every minimal normal subgroup of a group is characteristically simple. This follows from the fact that a characteristic subgroup of a normal subgroup is normal.
